#5335. Cboe and Citadel Sue to Stop US Stock Perps Hours After the CFTC Approved Them: Why Hyperliquid’s $5 Billion-a-Day Market Has the Most at Stake

Cboe and Citadel want US stock perps blocked. Hyperliquid already trades $5B of them a day, and ICE wants to bring it onshore.

A group backed by Cboe and Citadel Securities sued the CFTC on Tuesday, November 3, to block stock perps hours after the regulator cleared them for US exchanges, a fight that could decide whether Hyperliquid’s $5 billion-a-day market reaches American traders. The approval named no offshore venue, but it was aimed at one.

CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said Americans should not be “forced to turn to offshore, and often unregulated, venues” to trade perpetual futures on individual stocks.

🇺🇸 A CBOE AND CITADEL SECURITIES-BACKED GROUP SUES THE CFTC TO BLOCK PERPETUAL FUTURES ON US STOCKS, THE SAME DAY THE CFTC APPROVED THEM pic.twitter.com/38PNXGcM5f

— The Wolf Of All Streets (@scottmelker) November 3, 2026

The biggest of those venues runs on Hyperliquid. Trade.xyz, its largest builder market, did $4.99 billion in volume over the past 24 hours across 142 contracts on stocks, indexes and commodities, with $4.42 billion in open interest.

Six days ago, NYSE owner ICE agreed to bring those markets to US traders through a CFTC-regulated exchange of its own. HYPE jumped as much as 21% that day, to $97.74, just short of its $97.96 record.

The lawsuit didn’t knock it over. HYPE dipped to $81.01 early Wednesday and was back at $85.93 by 08:00 UTC, up 2.8% in 24 hours.

So what is the lawsuit about, and what does it mean for perp DEXs like Hyperliquid?

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Best Low-Cap Crypto

Who gets to regulate single-stock perpetuals?  The Capital Markets Alliance, whose members include Cboe, Citadel Securities and the Healthy Markets Association, filed in federal court in Manhattan. It argues the contracts are security-based swaps, which belong to the SEC and are kept away from retail investors.

“This issue, however, is about investor protection for securities trading and the rule of law,” Cboe CEO Craig Donohue said.

The CFTC hit back. “Our markets should be governed by law, not litigation campaigns intended to block innovation,” a spokesperson said.

Four exchanges are waiting on the outcome. Kalshi filed first, on September 18, followed by Coinbase Derivatives, Bitnomial and Crypto.com’s North American Derivatives Exchange. CME Group is already suing the CFTC over Kalshi’s Bitcoin perpetual, approved in May.

DISCOVER: Ripple Prime Opens 24/7 RWA Perpetual Swaps: Institutional Capital Hits Tokenized Stocks and Commodities

Big enough to rival its crypto markets. Hyperliquid’s own crypto perpetuals did $7.14 billion over the same 24 hours, so trade.xyz’s markets made up about 41% of everything traded on the chain.

Indexes and oil lead, but single stocks fill most of the list:

Trade.xyz launched in October 2025 as the first market built on HIP-3, Hyperliquid’s system that lets outside teams list their own contracts. It now handles about 98% of HIP-3 volume and says it has processed $650 billion in total trading.

It is built for traders outside the US. Hyperliquid blocks US users on its own front end, and that is the gap Selig wants US exchanges to fill.

Very little for its markets today, and a lot for its path into the US. The case can’t touch trades on Hyperliquid itself. What it decides is whether American exchanges can compete for the same flow, and whether ICE can bring trade.xyz onshore.

The two outcomes cut in opposite directions:

Neither will happen soon. ICE’s exchange still needs its own CFTC approval, and neither company has given a launch date.

The first real test comes sooner. The court still has to decide whether to freeze the approval while the case runs. A freeze would stall US listings before Kalshi or Coinbase trade a single contract.

EXPLORE: HYPE Jumps +23% as CFTC Pathway Raises Hyperliquid US Market Hopes

HYPE has given back most of last week’s ICE spike. It hit $97.74 on October 29, slid back over the next few days, and now trades at $85.93, just above its 20-day EMA of $84.02.

For now, the fight over stock perps is about who can sell them to Americans. Hyperliquid already sells them to everyone else, $5 billion a day of it.

#5334. France budget rejection sidelines stablecoin tax, wallet reporting

Three adopted amendments, including stablecoin taxation and self-custody reporting, fall away but could be reintroduced in the Senate.

The French National Assembly rejected the 2027 state budget’s revenue section late Wednesday, removing crypto-related amendments from the version of the bill sent to the Senate.

The Assembly rejected the revenue section by a vote of 458–0 at first reading, with two abstentions, according to the official voting record. The revenue section covers government income, such as taxes.

After the rejection, the government will send the Senate the original budget text, without the crypto-related amendments adopted by lawmakers.

The proposals could still be reintroduced in the Senate and would need to survive the remaining budget process to become law.

Faustine Fleuret, global head of public affairs at lending protocol Morpho, told Cointelegraph before the vote that rejection of the revenue section could “result in the rejection of the entire bill in the National Assembly, including provisions adopted by way of amendments.”

The Assembly adopted three crypto-related amendments before rejecting the revenue section.

On Oct. 16, lawmakers adopted an amendment that would make gains from crypto-to-stablecoin conversions taxable.

On Tuesday, lawmakers adopted another amendment that would require taxpayers to disclose self-custodied crypto holdings totaling at least 100,000 euros ($112,000), with the threshold assessed on Dec. 31 of the tax year.

Another amendment would increase penalties from 10,000 euros to 50,000 euros for crypto platforms failing to provide information requested by tax authorities.

The Senate is scheduled to begin debating the finance bill on Nov. 20, followed by an examination of the revenue section’s articles on Nov. 23, according to its schedule.

#5333. XRP Ledger Activates New Amendment to Strengthen Network

The XRP Ledger (XRPL) network recently activated a new amendment that helps secure the network by resolving potential security weaknesses and making some existing functionalities more robust and reliable.

This latest amendment, called fixCleanup3_4_0, was activated on Nov. 4, bringing a series of technical updates that include fixes for token issuance, automated market makers (AMMs), lending functionalities, and other parts of the XRP Ledger network.

A fix for a potential security weak point related to token issuance on the XRP Ledger network is a critical aspect of the latest amendment.

As explained in the official documentation of the XRP Ledger network, this update addresses a potential weakness related to delegated permissions that could allow some accounts to issue tokens when they are only allowed to destroy them.

On the XRP Ledger, token issuers can grant permissions to other accounts to perform certain tasks. For example, a stablecoin issuer could delegate permission to burn tokens to another account when customers want to redeem them.

With the latest amendment, the XRP Ledger network addresses this security weakness by preventing a zero-balance, burn-only delegated payment from resulting in the issuance of new tokens.

On top of addressing token issuance permissions, there's more to the fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment.

As explained in the official XRP Ledger network documentation, the fixCleanup3_4_0 update brings several fixes to decentralized trading, asset management, and transaction processing.

For automated market makers (AMMs), this latest update prevents some invalid auction bids and makes some improvements to how liquidity withdrawals and token clawbacks work.

It also brings some fixes for potential unexpected calculation errors or rounding issues that could occur in some cases.

These changes are supposed to make things more predictable when it comes to liquidity pools and avoid potential failures that could happen in some cases.

Another significant aspect of these changes concerns Single Asset Vaults and the proposed native lending infrastructure on the XRP Ledger.

As explained, this amendment brings some improvements to how rounding is handled when assets enter or exit vaults.

The idea is to ensure that transactions do not result in more or fewer assets being transferred than they should.

#5329. Ripple Executive Reveals Massive Growth of Company's London Hub

According to Ripple's UK and Europe Managing Director, Cassie Craddock, Ripple’s London office has expanded significantly over the last decade to become Ripple’s largest international hub outside the U.S.

“When we moved into our current office in 2018, there were 2 floors, and a lot of empty desks. Now we’re on 3 floors and full on all the desks. We’re now over capacity,” she wrote on X.

Craddock's comments came after she took part in a fireside chat at the British Residence in New York as part of Ripple’s Swell conference.

She revealed that Ripple chose to focus on London early on, given the UK's strong capital markets, mature legal system, experienced regulators and concentration of financial talent.

However, she added that regulatory uncertainty had previously limited the company’s capacity to build more relationships with leading U.K. financial institutions.

Ripple's story in the U.K. capital began on March 21, 2016, when the San Francisco-based company officially announced the launch of its first office in London, located in Canary Wharf.

Back then, the expansion was meant to accommodate the growing interest of European banks in distributed ledger technology and cross-border settlement solutions.

Ripple incorporated its U.K. entity in April 2016 under the name Ripple Europe Ltd. (later changed to Ripple Markets UK Ltd. in August 2022).

Ripple continued to expand its ties to U.K. financial institutions in the following years.

In April 2018, Santander introduced its new international payments app, One Pay FX, which used Ripple’s xCurrent technology.

In February 2022, Ripple announced a partnership with London-based payments company Modulr to make it easier to send cross-border payments to the UK and Europe.

Moreover, Ripple has played a role in developing the research landscape for blockchain in the U.K. In January 2026, Ripple shared that it had pledged more than £5M to UK universities under its University Blockchain Research Initiative.

One of the major milestones for Ripple in the U.K. occurred on Jan. 9, when Ripple received an Electronic Money Institution license and cryptoasset registration from the Financial Conduct Authority. The authorizations enabled Ripple to extend its regulated cross-border payment services to UK institutions.

In February, Ripple also secured a partnership with Aviva Investors to explore the tokenization of traditional investment funds.

This work resulted in the launch of a tokenized share class of Aviva Investors’ £22bn Sterling Liquidity Fund on the XRP Ledger on Oct. 26.

#5325. JPMorgan Projects Bitcoin To Outperform Stocks And Gold With 10% Annual Return Over The Next Decade

JPMorgan sees Bitcoin outperforming US stocks and gold in the next decade. The prediction is notable, as the bank has historically been cautious on BTC.

In a report published today, JPMorgan Asset Management made a bold prediction: Bitcoin will outperform gold and US stocks over the next decade. This bullish projection from a global banking giant further legitimizes Bitcoin as a strong investment alternative to traditional safe-haven assets.

According to the new report, JPMorgan forecasts Bitcoin to outperform gold, US stocks, and bonds with 10% annualized returns over the next 10 to 15 years. The bank expects BTC to beat gold and stocks over the long term, giving investors new confidence in the cryptocurrency.

Despite Bitcoin’s high volatility, the institution expects BTC to deliver a 10% annual compound return over the next 10 to 15 years, outperforming real estate, gold, and US stocks.

In its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions report today, October 20, JPMorgan predicts Bitcoin’s compound annual return at 10%. The report also estimates an arithmetic return of 20.9% and an annualized volatility of 55%.

The forecast outlook places Bitcoin ahead of many traditional investments in terms of compound annual return. The bank anticipates US large-cap stocks to return 7.5% yearly. It also expects gold to deliver a 5.5% annual return while projecting U.S. real estate investment trusts (REITs) to return 8.2% annually.

These projections suggest JPMorgan sees more robust long-term return potential in Bitcoin than in the other major asset classes mentioned above.

Despite the positive outlook, the bank sees higher volatility in Bitcoin, estimating BTC’s annualized volatility at 55% versus 17.2% for gold. This provides Bitcoin with opportunities for massive gains, but also substantial losses.

This is the first time that JPMorgan has included Bitcoin in its long-term return forecast in the 31-year history of its annual report. This shows a change of heart after years of criticism from the bank’s CEO.

Matt Hougan, Bitwise CIO, has celebrated JPMorgan’s Bitcoin forecast, terming it another milestone in the asset’s acceptance.

The development suggests that Bitcoin is becoming an important asset that JPMorgan doesn’t want to ignore. This shift highlights a wider change in attitude on Wall Street, including from JPMorgan’s CEO, Jamie Dimon, who has historically been skeptical of Bitcoin.

#5324. South Korea seeks 4th crypto tax delay, targets 2029 start

South Korea is seeking a fourth delay to its 22% crypto tax, months after reaffirming plans to begin taxing digital asset gains in January 2027.

South Korea’s government has backed postponing tax on cryptocurrency gains by another two years to 2029, in what would be the fourth delay to its implementation.

Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il announced the proposal Thursday, saying the government would consult lawmakers on postponing the January 2027 implementation date.

The tax would impose a 22% levy, comprising a 20% income tax and 2% local tax, on annual crypto gains exceeding 2.5 million won ($1,860).

The government cited 2029 as the start of information exchange with the US under the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF). It said imposing the tax before those exchanges begin could put the domestic market at a disadvantage relative to overseas markets. It also wants to account for changes under planned digital asset legislation.

Officials also said they plan to introduce a three-year loss carryforward provision, allowing investors to offset crypto losses against profits earned over the following three years. The government plans to submit amendments to improve the tax system during parliament’s regular session in 2027, with detailed tax guidelines planned for the first half of 2028.

The tax was originally scheduled to take effect in January 2022 but was subsequently postponed to 2023, 2025 and 2027.

The proposal reverses the government’s previous position. A Finance Ministry official said in May that implementation would proceed in 2027.

South Korean finance officials recently engaged with major crypto exchanges amid growing calls to postpone the tax. Industry representatives cited unresolved tax rules for different transaction types and insufficient time to prepare the necessary infrastructure.

#5322. Binance's CZ Sounds Alarm Over New Crypto Phishing Scam

Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ) has warned about a malicious crypto phishing scheme that uses a fake Trust Wallet website to lure unsuspecting users into connecting their wallets.

CZ shared a warning about a fraudulent website with a fake domain that mimics the popular Trust Wallet website.

Attackers modified the website domain by replacing the “u” with “a” and changing the extension from “.com” to “.cam,” which may trick unsuspecting users who don’t carefully inspect the domain.

The malicious website tricks users into connecting their crypto wallets in order to review their transfers.

However, the site contains JavaScript code that attempts to scan wallet balances using a backend API in order to prepare transfers to specific wallet addresses.

The attacker’s setup works with multiple well-known crypto wallets such as Trust Wallet, Phantom, and OKX Wallet.

CZ’s warning comes shortly after a surge in crypto phishing attempts against wallet users.

On Nov. 3, cybersecurity firm Bitdefender announced that scammers had started using the recent Binance security breach to spread fake emails impersonating Trust Wallet.

The phishing emails suggested that Trust Wallet users were also impacted by the Binance security breach. Therefore, they instructed users to perform a mandatory wallet verification procedure.

The email messages warned that users would be suspended after Nov. 7 if they did not complete the wallet verification process.

Bitdefender said that the phishing scheme affected users in multiple countries, including the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, Ireland and South Africa.

The phishing messages led users to fake verification websites where their wallet credentials or recovery data could be leaked.

Earlier this year, cybersecurity analysts from CYFIRMA spotted another phishing attack against Trust Wallet users. The attackers used malicious QR codes on Telegram to target Trust Wallet users.

He also argued that artificial intelligence could create new demand for cryptocurrencies as autonomous agents increasingly conduct economic activity.

“Yeah, I’m still very very bullish. You know, the next 24 months that Bitcoin will reach $250,000,” Hoskinson stated.

His forecast comes as Bitcoin faces questions about its near-term direction, with traders watching key price levels for signs of a recovery or a deeper correction.

Beyond Bitcoin’s price outlook, Hoskinson pointed to the growing relationship between artificial intelligence and blockchain technology as a potential source of demand across the crypto market. He argued that AI agents will need digital assets to transact, pay for services and participate in online marketplaces. Cryptocurrencies, particularly stablecoins, could provide the financial infrastructure for these activities.

“For agents to have agency and for agents to have economic identity has to be crypto,” he said.

Hoskinson believes AI-driven commerce could expand the practical uses of blockchain networks beyond speculative trading. He also suggested that combining crypto with AI could significantly increase transaction volumes across several digital assets.

#5317. Ripple CTO David Schwartz Explains Why XRP Could Gain Value as XRPL Adoption Grows

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has argued that rising adoption of the XRP Ledger (XRPL) could translate into stronger demand for XRP, pointing to the token’s role in liquidity, trading, and network transactions.

In an October 23 exchange on X, Schwartz challenged the idea that the ledger could become a major financial platform without its native asset gaining meaningful demand.

“The thesis is this: Low fees and reliable operation make XRPL a great place to move and hold value. That drives value flow to XRPL. XRP captures some of that value because of its unique advantages over other assets on XRPL,” Schwartz wrote.

He further noted that XRP has several advantages that could help it benefit as more financial activity moves onto the network. These include its role as a liquidity bridge between assets, its availability to accounts without counterparty risk, and its use to pay transaction fees.

“I think that’s one example of the mechanism I’m talking about. XRP has other advantages on XRPL too. It’s the only counterparty-free asset that any account can accept. People have to hold it to pay fees. All of those things can help drive value and demand,” he added.

Notably, the ledger’s built-in decentralized exchange can route trades through XRP when doing so offers a better exchange rate than trading two assets directly. If XRPL supports more markets and tokenized assets, XRP could therefore see greater use in connecting liquidity across those markets.

Schwartz said a scenario in which XRPL becomes highly successful in financial applications while XRP fails to attract strong demand is “very unlikely.” He acknowledged that a world dominated by a single settlement asset could produce a different outcome, but said he considers that possibility unlikely.

He also gave a hypothetical example involving Bitcoin. According to him, even if Bitcoin became the dominant settlement asset, wrapped or bridged versions of BTC could still trade on XRPL, creating opportunities for XRP to facilitate exchanges.

That said, on-chain data also offer another measure of adoption. Santiment reported last Thursday that the XRP Ledger had reached a record 8.24 million non-empty wallets, while daily wallet creation climbed to 4,772, its fifth-largest spike since March. This suggests that participation on XRPL has continued despite price volatility, which could generate sustained upward pressure on XRP.

Moreover, the firm identified $1.40 as an important level to watch, with a sustained move above it potentially opening the way toward $1.50 if wallet growth remains strong. Conversely, it warned that a drop below $1.30 alongside slower wallet creation would weaken the short-term adoption signal.

Some analysts have offered substantially more bullish price projections. Recently, Egrag Crypto said XRP appeared positioned to extend toward a macro target above $15, citing a chart pattern based on previous periods of price compression and breakout.

At press time, XRP was trading at $1.31, up 2.91% in the past 24 hours.

#5315. Laurent Correia on the Crucial Difference Between Earning Wealth and Holding Onto It

Laurent Correia treats making money and keeping it as two separate skills. After years in business and Dubai property, he says the second one took him much longer to learn.

A good month in business feels like a turning point. Invoices get paid, sales pick up, and plans that looked a bit fanciful a quarter ago start to seem doable. Then a few months pass, and you’re under the same pressure to keep earning as before.

Often the issue isn’t how much came in. Each rise in income tends to bring a new commitment, whether that’s a bigger team or higher personal spending, and by the end there’s little left to show for the good stretch.

Laurent Correia describes making money and keeping it as two different skills. Having worked across business ventures and property investment, he says the second took him longer to learn.

Revenue is the number most business owners watch because it’s right there. A completed sale proves a customer was willing to pay, and a few strong months make it tempting to decide the idea has found its audience.

It leaves a lot out, though. Operating expenses, commitments you’ve already made, and the cost of simply keeping the business running all come out of that figure before anything is left over. You can run a growing operation and still have very little room to move.

Correia’s distinction gives you a second question to ask after a sale: what has this income made possible beyond the sale itself? You don’t need a complicated model to answer it. Could the business get through a quiet month? Could it handle an unexpected bill without panic? Can the owner make a decision without waiting for the next payment to land?

None of that shows up in turnover, but it tells you a lot more about whether things are getting better. Plenty of owners earn more every year and still feel just as stretched because the extra money goes out as fast as it comes in.

Property became central to Correia’s longer-term thinking, with Dubai at the center of that activity. He describes the move toward owning assets as a major stage in going from entrepreneur to investor.

What stands out to me is the change in timescale. Running a business mostly means reacting to what’s in front of you this week. Deciding what the proceeds should pay for over the next several years is a different kind of thinking, and it raises questions that day-to-day trading never does.

The answers depend on the person. The SEC’s guide to asset allocation says your choices should depend on how long you have before you need the money and how much risk you can stomach. Both of those are personal.

Correia’s path shows how one person worked it out, but your situation isn’t his, so it won’t copy across cleanly. What you can take from it is a habit: let the future shape what you do now. Words like freedom or security don’t mean much until you pin them to something.

For instance, how many months of bills you’d want covered, or what you’d like to do without worrying about it. Write that down, and you’ve got something to plan around.

Correia says becoming a father changed what success means to him. These days his ambition is tied up with freedom, security and what he can leave his children.

That makes earning versus keeping money feel personal. A target carries more weight when it’s attached to something you want your work to pay for, and a bare number usually isn’t.

Try it on your own last good stretch. Set the income figure aside and ask what actually got better. You might have more breathing room, or rely less on one large customer, or find you can plan further out than before.

If nothing comes to mind, that tells you something as well, and it’s a decent starting point for your next goal. Instead of just aiming higher, ask what a good year ought to leave you with.

The next sale will always need attention, and so will whatever you do with the money after it.

Polygon developers now propose a step that has long been considered an absolute taboo in the crypto industry. They put to a vote a plan to rescue Binance and Polymarket money, and this plan is, to say it mildly, radical — zero out the hackers’ wallets at the protocol level. Ongoing cybersecurity crisis shows no signs of stopping, and now the industry is being faced with an uncomfortable choice: save systemic players or protect the inviolability of Web3’s main rule that transactions cannot be reversed. The Polygon PoS hard fork involves seizing 70.49 million POL tokens ($6.5 million at the time of the attack) from the hacker addresses to return them to the victims.

The crisis unfolded at the end of October after two independent hacks. The stolen assets were scattered across five wallets (23.86 million POL was taken from Polymarket, 46.63 million from Binance). Yes, Polygon validators immediately blacklisted the addresses, cutting off the outflow, but this is just an attempt to hold back the dam with bare hands. Manual blocking is a temporary plug, and the authors of the proposal openly admit it.

The hacker is not giving up either and is continuously bombarding the network with transactions carrying wild fees of up to 219,000 POL, counting on automation or a validator with a weakness for easy money to let the operation through for a windfall profit. Things have gone as far as direct attempts to bribe validators with cash, and the hacker simply ignored on-chain negotiations. The developers’ logic is simple: keeping millions in a manual “ban” forever is a dead end that leaves the entire network under constant fire.

No one has access to the hacker’s private keys, so Polygon is changing the consensus rules themselves. Should the hard fork get approval at a certain block, the hackers’ balances will be zeroed out, and an equivalent amount will be mirror-credited to verified Binance and Polymarket wallets — without any token printing.

Polygon Labs is well aware that such an administrative step completely negates the very idea of decentralization.

This plan inevitably triggers a strong sense of the notorious The DAO hard fork of 2016. Back then, to save the young Ethereum ecosystem, developers also had to go through a painful split of the community and ignore the “Code is Law” principle. But Polygon Labs hopes that in their case consensus among validators is already rock-solid, so they are narrowing the framework of the precedent as much as possible, positioning the fork as an exclusively one-time action.

The fate of the millions in POL token is being decided right now in a community vote. The largest validators are already in favor, since both platforms are critically important to Polygon’s survival. If the plan is approved, the software will be released after two weeks of testing, and exchanges and node operators will have to urgently update. Those who refuse to switch to the new code face automatic isolation on the old branch of the blockchain — with no connection to the main network.

#5310. As Binance Battles $6.3B Hack Fallout, Coinbase Reveals 99% of Customer Crypto Assets Are in Cold Storage

Questions about the safety of funds held on centralized exchanges have resurfaced following one of the crypto industry’s most alarming security incidents. As investors reassess the risks of keeping their holdings on trading platforms, Coinbase, America’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, is moving to reassure customers that its security measures make it harder for a similar breach to occur on its platform.

The platform is highlighting a key part of its protection strategy, disclosing that more than 99% of customer assets are kept in cold storage, with only a small fraction exposed to online systems. The disclosure offers a glimpse into how Coinbase approaches asset protection amid heightened scrutiny of exchange security.

Coinbase says its approach to safeguarding customer funds goes beyond simply keeping most holdings offline. The exchange maintains that over 99% of customer assets are stored in cold wallets, while distributed private keys, withdrawal restrictions, and systems designed to detect unusual activity provide additional layers of protection against unauthorized transactions.

In a blog post published Wednesday, Coinbase also clarified that it was not impacted by the Binance security incident. The exchange emphasized that customer holdings are maintained on a 1:1 basis and remain the property of their owners. It added that these assets are neither lent out nor used without customer authorization.

Beyond its cold-storage strategy, Coinbase outlines several additional security measures designed to give customers greater control over their accounts. According to its security page, the exchange supports two-factor authentication and hardware security keys, while its Coinbase Vault feature adds another layer of protection by allowing users to require multiple approvals before withdrawals can be completed.

Coinbase stressed that security remains an ongoing priority as emerging technologies reshape the threat landscape. The exchange said its responsibility is to keep “improving safeguards” and “continuously monitor for threats” to protect customers. It also pointed to the rapid advancement of AI, noting that it is changing the security environment and making continued investment in “best-in-class security innovation” increasingly important.

Coinbase also maintains a separation between customer holdings and its own corporate assets, reinforcing the distinction between funds belonging to users and those controlled by the company. In its latest quarterly filing, the exchange disclosed that its platform held approximately $377 billion in assets. By comparison, Coinbase reported $8.6 billion in corporate cash and another $2.2 billion in crypto assets held on its own balance sheet.

Coinbase’s statement comes days after the October 29 Binance heist, which saw approximately $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from the exchange’s internet-connected hot wallets. In an update posted Wednesday, Binance announced that it had replenished 98% of the affected assets using its own funds. The exchange also expanded its proof-of-reserves coverage to include 44 cryptocurrencies, highlighting its efforts to reassure customers about the security and backing of their holdings.

In a separate incident, Brazilian cryptocurrency exchange Mercado Bitcoin also suspended withdrawals following a reported $45 million hack, adding to growing concerns about the security of centralized trading platforms.

The amount is the first clue. Trump Media’s second-quarter 10-Q says 4,260.73 BTC served as collateral for its convertible notes, with restrictions lifted “no later than” May 29, 2028. Thursday’s two transfers add up to 4,259.35 BTC, and both sending wallets are now empty.

It mined about 891 BTC in the quarter but only kept about 425 of them, because it “sold a portion of Bitcoin production to cover operating costs.” That is a miner paying its bills, not a treasury exit.

#5307. South Korea Announces Delay in Crypto Taxation Policy

South Korea announced a delay in the introduction of its cryptocurrency capital gains tax until 2029, extending the tax-free period by two years as authorities plan on strengthening regulatory oversight and connecting data from exchanges with the United States, yna.co.kr reports.

Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il announced the proposal Thursday, acknowledging that the government would be postponing the controversial tax for a fourth time already.

Originally, the policy was scheduled to become active in January 2022: it would impose a 22% tax, local income tax on all cryptocurrency-related gains that exceed 2.5 million won.

While the proposed delay could provide a relief for the South Korean cryptocurrency market and even support the domestic trading activity, it remains a substantial risk factor for both local and overseas investors.

Officials argue that implementing the tax before international information-sharing systems become operational could disadvantage local exchanges and complicate enforcement against overseas trading activity.

Future tax liabilities aren't going to be eliminated, additional time to develop a comprehensive taxation network is more likely to enforce even more limitations on investors in the future, rather than a premature implementation with various legal loopholes.

The government also intends to introduce provisions allowing investors to carry forward cryptocurrency investment losses for up to three years, potentially reducing taxable gains in subsequent periods.

South Korea is also going to establish a separate working group that is going to further refine taxation rules and hopefully simplify reporting requirements for investors, considering the complexity of reporting digital assets transactions and traders on exchanges.

Legislative amendments are expected to reach the National Assembly in 2027.

Authorities reported the continuous coordinating with the Financial Services Commission to accelerate digital assets legislation, providing more transparency and investors protection.

For the industry in general, the proposed extension is more of a transition stage that should improve the competitiveness of the digital assets market, despite introducing stricter tax enforcement. Unfortunately for retail investors, it creates another barrier that might push fresh funds further away from the industry.

#5306. Top Wallet-as-a-Service Providers for Ethereum in 2026

Disclaimer: The below article is sponsored, and the views in it do not represent those of ZyCrypto. Readers should conduct independent research before taking any actions related to the project mentioned in this piece. This article should not be regarded as investment advice.

How Aligned, Privy, Dynamic, Turnkey, and Magic compare

A small group of established providers leads wallet-as-a-service solutions (WaaS) on Ethereum, including Aligned, Privy, Dynamic, Turnkey, and Magic. All are non-custodial and primarily compete on four things: how they secure the key, how they handle accounts and gas, how much of the stack they cover, and who owns the company.

For a consumer app or a financial institution building on Ethereum, the wallet is the integration you most want to get right the first time. It’s what users touch directly and trust with their funds, and it signs every transaction they make. It’s also the decision that compounds: once people hold balances, switching providers means migrating live accounts, so getting it right early pays off most.

Today’s leading WaaS providers look almost identical on the surface. They’re all non-custodial, and they all spare users the crypto mechanics: no seed phrase, no gas token, no contract prompts to approve. The differences that shape an integration sit underneath: the key-security model, how accounts and gas work, how much of the stack comes from one vendor, and who owns that vendor.

The field of credible wallet providers is small but far from uniform. Each was built around a different priority, and they overlap enough to blur together. Understanding what each one is keeps the biggest name from standing in for the best fit.

Aligned: Independent, founded by the team behind LambdaClass, and the only provider in the group focused exclusively on Ethereum: it runs on Ethereum L1 and on ZK rollups built with ethrex, while the others prioritize multichain reach. Every account is an EIP-7702 smart account that requires two signatures: one from the user’s key on their device and one from Aligned’s backend. It ships as part of a larger stack, with the rollup, proof aggregation, and interoperability all coming from the same team. Sovra runs identity for 8M+ people on it.

Privy (Stripe): The most widely deployed of the group by self-reported counts, with 200M+ accounts and customers like Hyperliquid and Ramp. It splits each key into two Shamir shares, both held on Privy’s side (one inside a secure enclave), and reassembles the key only inside the enclave. Its default EOA wallet can be upgraded in place through EIP-7702, or act as the signer of a separate ERC-4337 smart wallet. It carries several independent audits plus SOC 2 Type I and Type II.

Dynamic (Fireblocks): As much a login-and-wallet-connection platform as an embedded wallet, with a wide range of sign-in methods and connectors to 800+ external wallets. That fits apps where plenty of users already have a wallet, alongside those who need one made. Its keys use threshold-signature MPC. Customers have included Kraken and Ondo.

Turnkey: The signing and key-management foundation other wallets build on. It generates and uses raw private keys inside secure enclaves, with a policy engine that checks every signature. Of the enclave-based providers, Turnkey is the one that lets you verify the enclave itself: reproducible builds and remote attestation confirm the exact code that touched the key. Independent, founded by an ex-Coinbase Custody team. Customers include Bridge and Polymarket.

Magic: The oldest of the group, launched in 2018 and known for email-first onboarding. It protects keys with a mix of secure enclaves, a cloud key-management service, and sharding, and it holds the widest set of compliance certifications in the group: SOC 2, SOC 3, and ISO 27001. Its wallet business is being acquired by Payward, Kraken’s parent company, in a deal agreed in July 2026.

Most top WaaS solutions today are non-custodial, meaning they can’t move users’ funds without their consent. But that label covers a wide range: how much you trust the provider depends on how it handles the private key, and that trust underpins what you can promise users about their money. The clearest divide is whether the full key is ever assembled in one place, and it splits these solutions into two camps.

All three bring the full key together inside secure hardware, and they differ only on when. Privy splits it into two Shamir shares (not MPC), both held on its side, and reassembles them in a TEE at signing. Magic does the same with a TEE, a cloud key-management service, and sharding. Turnkey skips reassembly, keeping raw keys inside secure enclaves full-time behind a policy engine. Either way, the enclave exposes the full key, so its integrity is the security boundary.

Each gives you a different way to trust that boundary. Turnkey makes the enclave verifiable through open-source enclave code, reproducible builds, and remote attestation, so you can confirm the exact code handling the key. Privy leans on outside audits from Cure53, Zellic, and Doyensec, and Magic on the widest set of certifications in the group, SOC 2, SOC 3, and ISO 27001.

Dynamic and Aligned take the enclave out of the picture: no single key can move funds on its own, and they get there two ways. Dynamic uses threshold-signature MPC, where independent parties each hold a share and sign jointly, so no machine, Dynamic’s included, ever holds a spendable key. Aligned uses two separate keys and requires both to sign. The user’s key stays on their device (a WebAuthn passkey, a P-256 key, or an ECDSA key), Aligned’s key stays on its backend, and the account contract checks both signatures on-chain before it executes anything. Passkeys are verified on-chain as P-256 signatures inside the WebAuthn envelope. A breach of Aligned’s backend doesn’t move funds, and neither does a stolen device on its own.

The trade-off to plan for is availability: a signature needs a second party online. The two handle that differently. Dynamic’s 2-of-3 option lets any two of the three shares sign, so one being offline won’t lock the wallet. Aligned’s 2-of-2 doesn’t have that cushion: every transaction needs Aligned’s co-signer, so access depends on its backend staying reachable. For lost devices, Aligned offers optional guardian recovery: the guardian is set per app, and the timelock per account. The guardian can add a new key to an account, but that key can’t sign until a timelock expires (1 to 14 days, fixed when the account is created), which leaves a window to cancel an unwanted recovery. Accounts created without a timelock have no guardian.

One more point of trust sits above the accounts themselves. Aligned accounts route through a beacon contract, one per app, and the beacon’s owner can rotate the signers and point accounts to a new implementation without touching each one. That makes upgrades and key rotation simple to operate, and it means teams should know who controls the beacon for their app.

On its own, an Ethereum account is bare: a user needs ETH to do anything, every action is a separate approval, and losing the key means losing the funds. Account abstraction lifts those limits by giving the account programmable logic, so a product can cover gas for users, batch several steps into one confirmation, and offer recovery. All of them do this. They differ in the underlying standard, and providers are split between them.

ERC-4337 is the longest-running route, and Privy’s smart wallets build on ERC-4337. It works entirely at the application layer: user actions become “UserOperation” objects that a separate mempool and “bundler” services collect, batch, and submit through a shared EntryPoint contract, with an optional paymaster covering gas. Because it needs no change to Ethereum itself, it went live on Ethereum mainnet in March 2023 and now has the deepest audit and tooling history of any account-abstraction approach.

That maturity comes with operational overhead. Each user needs a separate smart-contract account deployed and maintained, and much of the market reaches 4337 through shared third-party middleware such as ZeroDev. It’s a well-worn path, and it also puts a common external layer in the critical signing path for many apps at once, which is worth weighing at institutional scale.

Aligned builds on EIP-7702, a 2025 protocol change that landed in Ethereum’s Pectra upgrade. It lets an ordinary account (an EOA) point to contract code and run it directly, so a user’s existing address gains smart-account behavior without deploying a second account alongside it. Aligned uses 7702 on its own, with no 4337 EntryPoint, bundler, or paymaster: its backend submits each transaction and pays the gas, so users never need to hold ETH or the chain’s native token. The result is leaner: one address, nothing extra to deploy or fund, and no third-party middleware between the user and the chain. Because it depends on 7702, it runs only on chains that have adopted Pectra.

EIP-7702 and ERC-4337 aren’t mutually exclusive: Privy signs 7702 authorizations for any implementation, Dynamic and Magic now offer 7702-based smart accounts, and Turnkey, as a pure signer, handles both transaction types and leaves the account model to you. Which one fits depends on whether a team wants established 4337 tooling or a simpler account with fewer moving parts.

Providers also differ in how much of the wallet you build yourself. The options fall on three levels, from a bare signing primitive you wrap in your own code to a full stack that arrives assembled. Where a provider sits decides how many vendors you take on and how independent the pieces of your stack stay.

Turnkey sits lowest, by design. It hands you a signing and key-management foundation and leaves the account-abstraction layer, gas handling, and smart-account logic for you to build. That’s the most work and the most control. Your wallet logic stays independent of any one chain or vendor, and signing sits behind a boundary you can attest. Teams with their own engineers often start here for that reason.

Privy, Dynamic, and Magic sit in the middle, as full embedded-wallet SDKs. They handle onboarding, key security, and gas, while you bring the chain and settle wherever you like. Dynamic leans hardest into authentication and wallet connection, with 800+ external-wallet connectors, so it suits apps where many users show up with a wallet already.

Aligned sits at the other end and sells the most in one piece: the wallet plus a rollup and proof aggregation, with interoperability, all from one team. Its ZK rollups are built with ethrex, the Rust Ethereum client from LambdaClass, and settle on Ethereum. That folds several procurement and integration decisions into one, and removes the seams between those layers.

It also concentrates your dependencies. The wallet, chain, and settlement all come from one provider, so they move together on a single roadmap and a single uptime, and more of your stack rides on one vendor. An institution gets one supplier to vet, and one point of dependence to weigh in return.

A wallet provider is a long-term dependency, so the decision comes down to a few things each team has to settle: how much to trust a provider with key handling, how much of the account and gas experience to hand off, and how much of the stack to source from one vendor.

The demo won’t decide it for you, because they all deliver the same clean experience: no seed phrase, no gas token, a smooth login. Their real differences sit underneath, in the two choices hardest to reverse once users hold funds: how the key is secured, and how much of the product leans on a single company. Past that, the best fit depends on what you’re building and what stage it’s at.

#5305. Bitcoin Shrugs Off Midterms as Experts Say Democratic Sweep Was 'Priced In'

Bitcoin Shrugs Off Midterms as Experts Say Democratic Sweep Was 'Priced In'

Democrats flipped both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the U.S. midterms, handing President Donald Trump a major political setback.

Experts say this was not the "preferred outcome" for crypto markets and that it has increased "uncertainty" for future pro-crypto policy. However, after a brief dip, Bitcoin is up 1.6% over the past 24 hours and now sits at $78,277, per Decrypt data. Broadly, almost every top 100 crypto token by market cap is in the green for the day.

"I think the Democratic sweep was largely priced in going into the midterms," André Dragosch, head of research at Bitwise Europe, told Decrypt. "The downside risks were fairly limited going into these midterms as sentiment was already very bearish and there were already signs of seller exhaustion again. So, it is no surprise that we have seen this kind of V-shaped recovery on an intraday basis during the midterms."

Polymarket put odds of the Democratic Party sweeping both the House and Senate during the midterms at 65.5% at the start of the week. Dragosch said these odds meant that markets weren't shocked by Tuesday's results.

James Butterfill, head of research at CoinShares, agreed. "My sense is that Bitcoin had largely priced in a Democratic sweep, leaving room for a relief rally as uncertainty clears," he said in comments shared with Decrypt. "Therefore, the anticipated result need not trigger another sell-off."

"Crypto policy did not decide the midterms. The economy, gas prices, the Iran situation, and Trump's unmet promises did," Heslin Kim, co-founder and CBO of Zenith, told Decrypt. "Crypto policy was irrelevant to the broader voting pool, but it now has the baggage of all the egregious activity that was stirred up in our ecosystem associated with the Trump family."

Tim Sun, senior analyst at HashKey, told Decrypt that the results do "increase the uncertainty surrounding the progress of crypto policy," but that Bitcoin's price action means that the market doesn't interpret it as a "major negative catalyst."

Specifically, this may be because the midterm results don't mean the Democrats can roll back existing pro-crypto guidelines set out by the SEC and CFTC, Dragosch said. However, it does mean that going forward, the market cannot rely as heavily on Trump's "political tailwinds for momentum," Sun added.

It also complicates the picture for the Clarity Act, which would establish rules for crypto markets. The bill has been in limbo since it was introduced in 2025, with many Democrats opposing it due to Trump's crypto conflicts of interest.

Dmitry Machikhin, CEO of BitOK, predicted in a note shared with Decrypt that the Clarity Act will remain in limbo well into 2027, thanks to the midterm results.

"The greater concern is slower crypto reform," Butterfill said. "CLARITY faces a harder path, while investigations into Trump-linked ventures could consume political capital and generate uncomfortable headlines across the sector. But the administration remains in place, and existing regulatory progress, including GENIUS, does not simply disappear."

He expects U.S. exchanges, token issuers and businesses that rely on new regulatory permissions to be more sensitive to the result than Bitcoin, and said established, compliant operators could even gain if scrutiny falls disproportionately on weaker competitors.

"A Democratic Congress may even be good for the industry in one way," Marcin Kaźmierczak, co-founder and COO of RedStone, told Decrypt. "Crypto shouldn't depend on one political camp. Infrastructure has to work for whoever is in power and bring most value to the ecosystem participants. Finance is changing, and politics will not stop it."

Despite the switch-up in the House and Senate, Dragosch expects little to change over the next two years.

"I personally expect more disputes, disagreements, and simply more of 'nothing stops this train,'" he said, pointing to a lack of significant progress to rein in fiscal deficits. "We will probably remain in a fiscally dominant environment with increasing fiscal risks, which I think is ultimately a tailwind for hard assets like Bitcoin."

Instead, he believes macro factors "remain in the driver's seat for now." Specifically, he points to a potential upcoming pivot from the Federal Reserve as a response to "increasing risk" around the AI trade.

"This will likely cause renewed interest in debasement-resistant assets like Bitcoin," Dragosch said, "and will continue to drive institutional adoption via ETPs and treasury companies as well."

Butterfill also pointed to macro factors. "For Bitcoin, real yields, dollar liquidity and ETP flows still carry more weight than the elections," he said. "I would temper expectations for the pace of U.S. reform, while remaining constructive on institutional adoption. How Trump responds to being constrained is the less predictable part."

#5303. Bitcoin Mining Giant MARA Sparks Selling Concerns With $133 Million Transfer

Bitcoin mining behemoth MARA Holdings has again raised concerns over possible selling pressure on Bitcoin after it transferred around $133 million worth of BTC to multiple institutional crypto platforms.

According to data from blockchain analytics firm Lookonchain, MARA moved a total of 1,650 BTC (around $132.8 million) to platforms like Galaxy Digital, Copper, and others in the past 12 hours.

The latest transactions, which were first reported on Nov. 5, came a few weeks after a series of massive Bitcoin movements involving the publicly listed mining company.

It seems MARA is once again dumping Bitcoin, referencing recent transfers of massive amounts of BTC to trading platforms and custodians.

Nevertheless, it is possible that the transfers do not actually indicate that MARA has sold BTC.

It's worth noting that platforms like Galaxy Digital and Copper offer different services, including trading and custody, for institutional clients.

So it could be that MARA moved the assets for liquidity, collateral, or other purposes.

It's worth mentioning that the latest BTC movements come after a few similar transactions involving MARA throughout October.

On Oct. 9, MARA moved around 996 BTC ($81.13 million at that time) to a wallet linked to crypto platform Galaxy Digital.

The transaction prompted some speculation about possible BTC selling, though it didn't confirm whether Galaxy Digital actually liquidated the assets or not.

On Oct. 19, Lookonchain again identified some other transactions involving wallets linked to the Bitcoin miner.

As per the analytics firm's data, the wallets linked to the Bitcoin miner sent 1,000 BTC (approximately $82.8 million) to crypto exchanges like Binance.

Towards the end of October, concerns over possible selling increased.

Specifically, on Oct. 27, MARA moved another 1,000 BTC (around $80.19 million) to institutional crypto custody platform BitGo.

The following day, Lookonchain noted another transaction of 1,000 BTC, worth about $80.66 million, to BitGo.

As per its second-quarter financial disclosure, MARA sold around 23,093 BTC for $1.6 billion in the first half of 2026.

In the second quarter alone, MARA sold 2,213 BTC at an average price of $73,078.

Meanwhile, MARA has also made it clear that it is no longer interested in holding all the Bitcoin it mines.

#5302. Thailand to block Bitget in December over unlicensed crypto trading

Thailand’s SEC filed a criminal complaint against Bitget’s operator, with access to its website and app set to be blocked from Dec. 5.

[Update Nov. 6, 6:35 am UTC: This article has been updated to include a statement from a Bitget spokesperson.]

Thailand’s securities regulator has filed a criminal complaint against BG Limited, the operator of cryptocurrency exchange Bitget, for allegedly operating without a license.

Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said Thursday that it had notified the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society to block access to Bitget from Dec. 5. The restriction will cover Bitget’s website, other associated domains and its mobile app.

The regulator advised users to take action regarding assets held on the platform before the deadline.

The complaint follows Bitget’s Oct. 20 announcement of plans to acquire a licensed Thai crypto exchange.

A Bitget spokesperson told Cointelegraph that the exchange was reviewing the Thai SEC’s announcement and evaluating its options for engaging with the regulator.

“We have no further information to share at this stage,” the representative said, adding that user assets remain safe and that Bitget would provide guidance on any changes affecting access to its services via official channels.

According to the SEC, Bitget offered crypto trading services between 2022 and 2025, charged trading fees and promoted its services in Thai through its websites and social media channels. The regulator said these activities violated Thailand’s digital asset business licensing requirements.

The complaint also names Kritsana Kritsananuwat, whom the SEC accused of helping promote Bitget through Facebook and YouTube. The watchdog previously filed a criminal complaint against him in March 2025 over allegations that he helped promote OKX’s unlicensed exchange activities.

Cointelegraph attempted to contact Kritsananuwat through a phone number listed for advertising inquiries in a video on his YouTube channel but was unable to reach him.

Thailand introduced licensing requirements for digital asset businesses in 2018 and tightened the rules in April 2025 to cover foreign platforms targeting Thai users. Changes to a separate cybercrime law also made it easier for the ministry to block access to unlicensed platforms.

Related: Thailand SEC says several companies eye crypto ETFs, none has applied

The regulator filed the complaint with Thailand’s Economic Crime Suppression Division for investigation. Prosecutors will decide whether to bring charges, while courts will determine criminal liability.

Bitget announced plans on Oct. 20 to acquire GMO-Z.com Cryptonomics, a locally licensed crypto exchange and brokerage, through BTGT Management (Thailand), a company in which Bitget said it held an interest.

The proposed acquisition remained subject to regulatory approval and other conditions at the time of the disclosure. Bitget said it intended to introduce its trading platform to Thai users after completing the transaction and obtaining approval for the change of control.

“Thailand is an important part of Southeast Asia’s digital asset landscape, and this acquisition gives us a great opportunity to establish local operations,” Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said at the time.

Binance has revoked all API keys associated with SignalPlus after the digital asset trading infrastructure provider identified a potential security vulnerability, prompting the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange to take measures to protect users, according to the latest report on the Binance's official Square feed.

The exchange confirmed Thursday that the decision was intended to prevent possible unauthorized access through connections established between Binance accounts and SignalPlus. Binance emphasized that its internal systems had not been compromised and that customer funds remained safe.

Binance's security documentation advises users to revoke potentially compromised credentials immediately and restrict API permissions to necessary functions.

For affected SignalPlus users, restoring automated trading functionality may require generating new credentials once the integration is deemed secure.

SignalPlus provides trading infrastructure and analytical tools for cryptocurrency derivatives markets, allowing traders to manage positions and execute strategies across exchanges through API integrations.

These connections enable third-party applications to interact with exchange accounts without requiring users to transfer their assets off-platform. However, depending on the permissions granted, compromised API credentials can potentially expose accounts to unauthorized trading activity.

Binance has effectively severed existing integrations between its platform and SignalPlus. The measure could potentially disrupt automated trading strategies that rely on those connections.

Major cryptocurrency exchange Binance is witnessing a significant turnaround in capital flows, founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ) has claimed in a recent X post. The former CEO of the platform said the exchange has seen $2.8 billion in net inflows in the last 24 hours, a significant improvement after the latest hack that caused the platform to bleed funds for a while.

CZ, in an attempt to promote third-party reporting, retweeted a post by Mars BNB showing strong recovery flows into the cryptocurrency exchange. This is a sharp turnaround for the exchange, as it had continued to bleed funds for several days.

Binance experienced crypto’s largest hack in its history, worth roughly $6.3 billion, last week. The cryptocurrency exchange temporarily paused withdrawals while investigating the attack and updating its security infrastructure. Withdrawals resumed only on Sunday at the start of this month, and even then in phases to avoid a major episode.

The resumption of withdrawals, the release of proof of reserves, the freezing of more than $2 billion in stablecoins, and CZ’s immediate intervention helped mitigate a situation that could have easily spiraled out of control. Binance officials insist that the vast majority of affected assets (roughly 95%) are replenished, with major tokens such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, USDT, BNB, etc. set to have full backing. The exchange’s overall assets are worth around $171 billion, and it remains profitable.

Independent on-chain reporters like DefiLlama and others identified major outflows from the company in the immediate aftermath of the hack. However, the situation eventually changed for Binance, as later reporting put net inflows around $2.3 billion, still less than the $2.8 billion figure touted by CZ.

The swift reversal of the withdrawal trend shows that users still have confidence in the exchange’s operations despite the recent security fiasco. Schwartz picked the "right time" to step back from Ripple, but he's clearly not out of the game.

Ripple Chief Legal Officer Stuart Alderoty also weighed in on the election outcome, rejecting suggestions that the results represented a major defeat for the crypto industry.

Congratulating the newly elected lawmakers, Alderoty said Ripple was prepared to work with representatives from both parties to maintain America’s position as a leading destination for blockchain and digital asset businesses.

He highlighted Fairshake’s performance, a crypto-backed political action committee that supported candidates during the election cycle. According to Alderoty, the organization secured meaningful victories in both primary contests and the general election.

He further referenced preliminary figures from the Stand With Crypto initiative, which indicated that a substantial number of pro-crypto lawmakers had secured seats across party lines.

“Let me be clear — some headlines will call this a setback for crypto. The facts are far more nuanced,” Alderoty stated.

#5295. Morning Minute: CFTC Clears Stock Perps, Gets Sued the Same Day

Morning Minute: CFTC Clears Stock Perps, Gets Sued the Same Day

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

⚖️ CFTC Clears Stock Perps, Gets Sued the Same Day

A perpetual future is a leveraged bet on a price that never expires. You hold it as long as you can meet margin and keep paying a funding rate. It’s analog product would be options in TradFi, with a few differences (primarily no expiration date). Crypto traders have used them for years, mostly on offshore venues like Binance and onchain platforms like Hyperliquid, because U.S. law had no clear home for the product.

On Tuesday the CFTC said Americans can now trade them on individual stocks.

Hours later, Wall Street sued to stop it.

The approval came as a statement from CFTC Chairman Michael Selig. Equity perpetual futures are now tradable on CFTC-registered exchanges, classified as security futures products under the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000, which puts them under joint CFTC and SEC oversight.

The list of venues that can actually do this is short, and it was assembled quietly. A firm needs to be a CFTC-designated contract market and separately notice-registered with the SEC as a national securities exchange for security futures products. Seven entities hold both today: Cboe, CME, Coinbase, Kalshi, Bitnomial, Nadex, and ICE Futures U.S. Five of those seven filed inside a single 30-day window in September.

Kalshi is furthest along, with a filing covering 56 to 58 names and a launch expected within days. Coinbase has filed to list perps on Apple, Tesla and Nvidia. So those two are immediate winners. But Hyperliquid and Lighter, the top crypto perps protocols, are next in line for potential CFTC approvals and are likely future winners as well (LIT +10% on the day).

Then came the lawsuit. A new group called the Capital Markets Alliance filed in the Southern District of New York, naming Cboe, Citadel Securities and the Healthy Markets Association among its members. Its argument runs on two tracks.

The group wants the policy eliminated. The American Securities Association piled on separately, pointing out that Congress banned selling security-based swaps to retail investors at all.

A CFTC spokesman called the suit “troubling,” adding that “our markets should be governed by law, not litigation campaigns intended to block innovation.” The CME already tried this once, suing over the CFTC’s crypto perps approval on the theory that perpetuals are swaps rather than futures. That one went nowhere.

Well, remember that old phrase: “First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you, then you win."

We’re at the fight stage. Next stop, winning.

Speaking with Cointelegraph at SALT London, Scaramucci said the memecoin launches shortly before Trump’s January 2025 inauguration undermined bipartisan momentum for crypto regulation following the 2024 election.

“Singular reason,” Scaramucci told Cointelegraph when asked whether the memecoin activities were the sole reason the bill did not pass. He said Democrats who had become more receptive to crypto regulation withdrew their support following the launches.

The remarks follow the Senate’s failure to advance the CLARITY Act on Sept. 15, when a procedural motion received 49 votes in favor and 50 against, falling short of the 60 votes required. The bill, which sought to establish a federal regulatory framework for digital assets, faced disagreements over ethics provisions restricting government officials’ crypto interests.

Scaramucci also pointed to disagreements over proposed ethics restrictions, saying lawmakers sought stronger provisions that the White House opposed.

“I think it’s the business interests, the memecoins,” Scaramucci said, adding that lawmakers were “trying to put real teeth into the ethics provision” but the White House did not want to sign it.

“There’s culpability on both sides for that deal not going forward,” he said.

Related: Market participants weigh in on SEC’s proposed crypto regulations

In July, five Democratic senators called for hearings into Trump’s crypto holdings and potential conflicts of interest, citing concerns that his financial ties could influence crypto policy. House Financial Services Committee Chair French Hill also acknowledged that Trump’s crypto businesses had complicated efforts to pass legislation.

In August, consumer advocacy group Public Citizen estimated that investors incurred at least $4.7 billion in largely unrealized losses across Trump-related crypto ventures, including $3.2 billion associated with the Official Trump (TRUMP) memecoin. #5291. Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Confirms Cyberattack After ZachXBT Ties It to $133M Crypto Theft

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Confirms Cyberattack After ZachXBT Ties It to $133M Crypto Theft

French banking group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa has confirmed that it was hit by a cyberattack that allowed fraudulent operations, a day after onchain investigator ZachXBT named it as the alleged victim of a crypto theft of more than $133 million.

In a statement shared with Decrypt on Wednesday, the bank said the incident was "closed and now under control," and that operations were resuming gradually after it put stronger security measures in place. It said customers' assets were not affected, and that the attack had only delayed the execution of some transfers.

The bank did not mention crypto or say how much was taken. The amounts affected are still being assessed, but are "in any event not of a nature to call into question the solidity and financial health of the group," it said, according to Decrypt's translation.

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa said it informed the relevant supervisory authorities as soon as it detected the attack, and temporarily suspended some transactions as a precaution to prevent further fraudulent movements. It also warned customers to watch out for phishing attempts following the attack. Decrypt has reached out to Crédit Mutuel Arkéa for further comment, including on whether the losses involved crypto.

"Disclosing the EU financial institution exploited for $133M+ is allegedly Credit Mutuel Arkea, a French bank with $235B in assets," ZachXBT wrote on his Telegram channel on Tuesday. "The attack on the bank occurred for multiple days. I suspect the amount stolen is larger when accounting for OTC activity."

In an update on Tuesday, he said he had identified a further $27 million in exchange withdrawals by the attacker, bringing the total to more than $133 million, and that some of those withdrawals took place after his initial disclosure. He also published four Ethereum addresses he said were linked to the theft.

"My working theory is a large financial institution in Western Europe was exploited and it's currently being covered up," ZachXBT wrote at the time, accusing it of not having conducted "proper incident disclosure" and thereby preventing law enforcement from freezing some $30 million in stolen funds.

He did not say how he had identified the bank, or how the attacker gained access to its exchange accounts.

The mutual banking group has been preparing to move into crypto. In May, French financial newspaper L'Agefi reported that it had applied for a license under MiCA, the EU's crypto rulebook, to offer crypto services to its retail customers and to provide them as a white-label service through its Arkéa Banking Services division.

The allegation comes days after the $6.3 billion hack of Binance, the largest crypto theft on record, which the FBI has attributed to North Korean hackers. ZachXBT said the attacker in the suspected EU theft remains unidentified, but that he could say "with a high degree of confidence it is NOT Lazarus Group," the North Korean hacking collective, "based on multiple laundering indicators."

This story has been updated to add comment from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa.

In his latest post on X, Ben-Sasson wrote that the crypto industry faces a key threat besides quantum computers. In particular, he pointed to the growing capabilities of AI as a tool for cybersecurity attacks.

The reason is that today, more than ever before, we rely on cryptography.

"Your crypto keys, your online life, any app that holds something important to you — it's all secured by cryptography," he wrote.

According to Ben-Sasson, the growing power of AI tools puts more pressure on wallet cryptography. This threat is more likely to become an issue before quantum computers pose a significant threat.

The Zcash co-founder also pointed out the need for stronger cryptographic standards. He specifically highlighted hash-based methods such as ZK-STARKs.

The discussion comes weeks after the infamous Binance hack. The incident resulted in around $6.3 billion in losses from the exchange's hot wallets.

Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals while investigating the breach. The exchange has since reported recovering around 95% of the affected assets.

AI hacker attacks have been on the rise in 2026. According to Google Threat Intelligence statistics, the monthly number of disclosed software vulnerabilities has nearly doubled over the past year.

This means that AI has already become a powerful scanner for potential system weaknesses.

For instance, Casa CSO Jameson Lopp pointed out that attackers can already use AI to automate the search for conventional software bugs and weaknesses in wallet firmware.

In other words, the discussion should be focused on more specific security vulnerabilities in existing software rather than a hypothetical future AI threat.

#5288. Wall Street’s Plumbing Goes Onchain as Morgan Stanley Tokenizes Securities

Wall Street’s Plumbing Goes Onchain as Morgan Stanley Tokenizes Securities

Morgan Stanley has started moving U.S. stocks and Treasuries onto blockchain rails, using Wall Street’s own plumbing to do it.

The bank said Tuesday that it’s among the first to tokenize real-world assets through the DTCC Tokenization Service, converting U.S. equities and Treasuries into tokenized form.

The service, which went live Oct. 28, is run by the Depository Trust Co., a subsidiary of the Depository Trust & Clearing Corp. The DTC is the post-trade backbone of U.S. markets, with more than $114 trillion in assets under custody.

“The hands-on experience of integrating tokenized securities with established market infrastructure will inform the continued development of the firm’s digital asset capabilities as the market evolves,” said Amy Oldenburg, Morgan Stanley’s head of digital assets strategy.

The service lets eligible firms convert securities held at DTC into tokenized “digital twins” and back again, delivering them to digital wallets of their choice. The tokens keep the same ownership rights, investor protections and economic entitlements as the originals, according to DTCC, and are designed to let firms move collateral and tap new pools of liquidity within minutes. The service currently runs on the Canton Network and DTCC’s private Besu network, with more blockchains planned for 2027.

Morgan Stanley is one of 20 DTC participants that have signed up so far, alongside Bank of America, Citi, J.P. Morgan, Fidelity Investments, Citadel Securities, and UBS, among others. DTCC said it developed the service with input from more than 150 firms.

The launch caps a regulatory path that began in December 2025, when the SEC gave DTC a no-action letter allowing it to tokenize Russell 1000 stocks, major index ETFs and U.S. Treasuries. DTCC has also worked with Chainlink on tokenized collateral management and laid out its plans for the service earlier this year as major Wall Street firms signed on.

The bank-led approach contrasts with crypto-native efforts to tokenize stocks. Fifty-six companies, including Tesla, SpaceX, Amazon, and Nvidia, have objected to having their shares traded on OKXICE TSV, a planned tokenized stock venue from OKX and NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange. Under the SEC’s innovation exemption, those objections bar the venue from listing third-party tokenized versions of their stock.

Demand is building, but the market is still young. The International Monetary Fund found last month that tokenized stocks trade mostly outside U.S. market hours, though they remain more volatile and less liquid than their traditional counterparts.

TL;DR: European Central Bank officials have discussed the planned move to T+1 securities settlement in October 2027 alongside longer-term work on tokenized settlement infrastructure. A future regulatory settlement date should not be confused with a finished network rollout.

The deadline matters most to firms that process transactions across several jurisdictions. They have to harmonise instructions, reconcile holdings and manage currencies while the clock gets shorter. Blockchain advocates should explain specifically which tasks become easier and which stay with regulated intermediaries.

European Central Bank officials have discussed the planned move to T+1 securities settlement in October 2027 alongside longer-term work on tokenized settlement infrastructure. A speech published October 29 outlined how shortening the conventional settlement cycle and experimenting with new technology fit into wider financial-market modernisation. The two projects are related strategic topics, not a statement that blockchain technology will automatically replace Europe’s existing settlement systems next year. The dated original disclosure is the starting point for the figures and product scope discussed here.

T+1 means most eligible securities trades settle one business day after the trade date, compared with a longer conventional cycle. Shorter cycles can reduce outstanding exposures and certain capital needs, but they compress the time available to resolve breaks, fund positions and coordinate across time zones. Tokenization addresses a different design question: how ownership records and money can move using new technical infrastructure.

The connection is operational discipline. A market trying to settle sooner needs robust automation, accurate records and predictable funding. Tokenized assets may eventually support more tightly connected workflows, but they are not necessary to achieve the near-term T+1 timetable. Existing post-trade institutions and banks still have crucial responsibilities.

A tokenized instrument must connect technical records with enforceable financial rights. Trading software can move a token quickly, but an issuer, custodian, transfer agent or settlement bank may still have to recognise the result. This is why tokenization announcements need to explain which part of the lifecycle is changing, not merely advertise that a blockchain is involved.

This development also connects to two subjects our newsroom has been following: DTCC’s tokenized securities infrastructure rollout and tokenized fund redemptions tested over a weekend. They explain related market structure and should not be mistaken for evidence that every new proposal is already live.

A future regulatory settlement date should not be confused with a finished network rollout. Different products and markets can have exclusions or distinct implementation rules. Nor should a policy speech be read as authorising every private tokenized security to circulate without existing investor-protection requirements.

Real settlement infrastructure is judged by whether it works on bad days, not just during presentations. Reconciliation, asset eligibility, funding, corporate actions and recovery from errors remain central. Continuous technical operation can improve coordination, yet it does not create market liquidity or remove the obligations of regulated participants.

Watch for detailed industry testing, bank funding arrangements and official updates on both T+1 readiness and central-bank-money experiments. The important measure is whether settlement failures and costs fall without shifting uncontrolled risk to participants. Europe’s timeline creates a concrete deadline, while the tokenization debate remains a longer-term architecture choice.
